cim: AI-Generated Evidence in Drug Discovery: Reliability, Legal Risk & FDA Compliance
cim_eredeti: AI-Generated Evidence in Drug Discovery: Reliability, Legal Risk & FDA Compliance
szoveg_eredeti:
AI models used in drug discovery and development are inherently probabilistic and can generate outputs that are plausible in form but wrong in substance, with direct consequences for regulatory submissions, clinical trial integrity, and legal liability.

The reliability problem is compounded by three structural flaws of AI/ML systems: training on incomplete or unrepresentative datasets; the opacity of AI reasoning; and high sensitivity to small changes in input data, which undermines experimental reproducibility.

Adversarial manipulation of training data represents an emerging legal and regulatory risk for sponsors and their AI vendors.

The life sciences sector is uniquely vulnerable to the inherent risks of AI-generated evidence in drug development and discovery. This client alert focuses on five core challenges: hallucinations, skewed predictions from unrepresentative training data, the opacity of AI reasoning, input sensitivity that undermines reproducibility, and adversarial manipulation of training data. To address these risks, companies should use experimental validation and human oversight as the common legal and regulatory safety net. This entails among other measures auditing AI outputs, characterizing training data, and structural oversight. Companies also should prepare for evolving frameworks and guidance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Union (EU) that address use of AI in drug discovery and development .

The use of AI in drug discovery and development generates a category of legal risk distinct from ordinary scientific uncertainty: AI/ML systems can err in ways that are both difficult to detect and difficult to attribute after the fact. These features create legal exposure across multiple domains. A regulatory submission that relies on AI-generated data without independent human validation may not meet existing FDA data integrity standards; a clinical trial dataset whose outputs were distorted by adversarial manipulation of the AI tool’s training data may expose the sponsor to product liability and regulatory fraud risk; and AI-generated expert analysis offered in litigation may be vulnerable to challenge on reproducibility grounds under Federal Rule of Evidence 702.

Across regulatory frameworks, international guidelines, and emerging liability regimes, the legal and regulatory backstop for AI-generated evidence is human review by a qualified person who can independently assess the accuracy and completeness of AI outputs.

What hallucinations are: An AI/ML model generates outputs by predicting the most statistically likely response based upon its training data and inputs provided. Thus, a model can produce an output that is misleading or completely fabricated yet presented with total confidence. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as hallucination.

The drug development context: In drug discovery and development, an AI/ML model may generate a fabricated biochemical reference that appears authoritative, a skewed efficacy prediction that reflects the limits of its training data rather than the biology of the molecule, or a result that may not be replicated when the same inputs are run again. This occurs because of inherent structural features of how the model processes data, not experimental errors.

Legal exposure: The legal consequences of undetected hallucinations vary by context. In regulatory submissions, AI-generated false data that is submitted to the FDA without independent verification may constitute a material misrepresentation under 21 U.S.C. § 331, irrespective of intent. In patent prosecution, fabricated prior art references submitted to the USPTO without verification abrogates the duty of candor under 37 C.F.R. § 1.56 — and a finding of inequitable conduct can render an issued patent unenforceable.

The structural problem: An AI model’s predictions are bounded by its training data. A model trained on an incomplete historical dataset that overrepresents certain molecular classes, patient populations, disease presentations, or experimental conditions will generate predictions that systematically reflect those gaps. The skew is often invisible from the output alone: a model can produce highly confident predictions that are precisely wrong in ways that trace entirely to what it was and was not trained on.

The regulatory consequence: FDA submissions that rely on AI-generated predictions derived from training data of unknown or uncharacterized provenance create data integrity risk. The FDA’s existing GCP and GMP frameworks require that data submitted in support of regulatory applications be accurate, complete, and traceable. The FDA-EMA Joint Guiding Principles of Good AI Practice in Drug Development (January 14, 2026), establish a unified framework for the entire product lifecycle. Through Principle 6 (Data Governance) and Principle 7 (Model Design), establishing that rigorous data provenance, processing traceability, and fit-for-use data are mandatory prerequisites to ensuring the generalizability and robustness of AI-driven evidence. ICH M15 — the final, harmonized international guideline on model-informed drug development adopted January 29, 2026 — provides a complementary framework, expressly covering AI/ML models used in drug development and establishing international expectations for model verification and validation that include characterization of training data limitations.

The traceability gap: Unlike conventional statistical models, many AI/ML models do not generate step-by-step, traceable outputs. Instead, inputs pass through complex layers of learned parameters to produce a result without human-readable intermediate steps. This is the “black box” problem: the output may be correct, but the path from input to output lacks explainability.

The regulatory dimension: The FDA’s existing expectation of traceable, auditable data — embedded in 21 C.F.R. Part 11, in GCP and GMP frameworks, and in the agency’s longstanding data integrity guidance — creates structural tension with AI opacity. ICH M15 addresses this directly, establishing harmonized international expectations for model transparency and documentation that include the obligation to characterize and disclose the limits of a model's explainability. The FDA-EMA Joint Guiding Principles similarly identify traceability as a core requirement for AI used in drug development, across the full product lifecycle.

The product liability dimension: The revised EU Product Liability Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/2853) expressly links disclosure and explainability to liability. If a manufacturer does not disclose or cannot explain how an AI system reached a particular output, the PLD creates a presumption that the product was defective. Companies must comply ahead of the December 9, 2026 transposition deadline, when the PLD becomes law in EU countries.

The reproducibility problem: AI/ML models can exhibit high sensitivity to small changes in input data, sometimes described as “brittleness.” A model that produces a specific output when given a particular input may produce a materially different output when such input is provided in a slightly modified format or version, not because of experimental variation but because of how the model’s learned parameters interact with the input at the margin. This creates a reproducibility problem. The experiment may have been run perfectly, but that the model’s outputs are structurally unstable at the input boundary.

The regulatory consequence: FDA and ICH frameworks expect that results submitted in regulatory applications be reproducible; that is, that the same data, processed through the same methodology, should yield the same results. Where an AI model’s outputs cannot be reproduced from substantively identical inputs, the model may not meet these standards.
